titleEn: The Secret History of the Mongols — §194: The Taunt at the Qachir and Tayang's Plan
part: §194 — The Taunt at the Qachir and Tayang's Plan
about: One long section of debate. Tayang Qan, at the Qachir in the Qanghai, hears the scouts' report and sends his son Küchülüg a plan: draw the Mongols back to the Altai and strike when their geldings are worn out. Küchülüg answers with a taunt, that Tayang is a woman who has never been farther than the tent, and the message wounds his father. Tayang praises his son's bravery; the old lord Qori-Sübechi then reproaches him with the example of Inancha-Bilge, who never showed his back, and with his mother Kürbesü, and rides off in disgust. The grammar to watch is the converb chain in -žu/-žü that carries the plan, the conditional -γasu, the reflexive -jan/-jen, the possessives in -tü/-tu, and the causative -ġül-. Several lines are hard, above all the image of the heavy woman and the calves, the junction of the twentieth and twenty-first units, and the sentence about Kürbesü. The notes say where. The Mongol readings follow Shiratori; the English is a first drafting.

sentences.t: Qaraγ̇ul-un ene kele kürtežü Tajaṅ Qān Qaṅγai-jin Qačir- Usun-a ažuγ̇ui.
sentences.l: Scouts' this word being-conveyed, Tajaṅ Qān, Qaṅγai's Qačir water-at was.
sentences.i: When this word of the scouts reached him, Tayang Qan was at the river Qachir in the Qanghai.
sentences.n: Qaraγul-un is 'of the scouts' (Ming 哨望的, 'lookout'), the genitive -un, and it hangs on kele 'word': 'the scouts' word'. kürtežü is a converb in -žü; the Ming 被到着 reads it as passive, 'being reached', so the word reaches Tayang rather than he fetching it; the stem kürte- is inferred from that Ming gloss. Qaṅγai-jin Qačir- Usun-a: the genitive -jin joins the Qanghai (Ming 地名的) to the river name; the printed hyphen after Qačir- is Shiratori's, and Usun-a is 'to the water' (Ming 水行) with -a, here 'at'. I read it as 'the river Qachir in the Qanghai'. ažuγui (Ming 有來) is the narrative past of a- 'be, stay'; the full stop closes the sentence. The scouts are the Naiman scouts who left at the end of §193.

morph.gloss: to be conveyed, to reach (passive, stem inferred from the Ming) [被到着]
qan, sovereign (short form of qaγan) [皇帝]
the Qanghai, a place [地名 的]

sentences.t: Ene kele kürġeġülüġed Küčülüg Qān köġün-dür(i)-jen keleležü ilerün;
sentences.l: This word having-conveyed, Küčülüg Qān son-to-own saying, going;
sentences.i: He had this word carried to his son Küchülüg Qan, and sent it with this message:
sentences.n: kürġeġülüġed is the converb 'having caused to reach' (Ming 敎到了, 'made to arrive'): -ġül- is the causative, -üġed 'having' (the ü a linking vowel). The subject is Tayang. köġün-dür-jen is 'to his own son' (Ming 子自的行): köġün 'son', -dür dative, -jen the reflexive-possessive 'one's own'. keleležü 'saying' (Ming 說着) and ilerün (Ming 去, 'go') are two more converbs. ile- may be 'go' or 'send' (the glossary is unsure), and I have taken 'sent word', which is a guess. The semicolon after ilerün leads into a speech, which I take to start with the next unit; Shiratori prints no opening quotation mark, only the closing one at the end of the message, so where it starts is my judgement (the alternative is that these lines are the scouts' report).

sentences.t: Moṅγol-un aγtas turuγad ažuγ̇ui.
sentences.l: Mongols' geldings lean were.
sentences.i: "The Mongols' geldings were lean.
sentences.n: aγtas is aγta 'gelding' with the plural -s; turuγad is turuγ 'lean' with the plural -ad (Ming 瘦每). Note that -un on Moṅγol-un is the genitive 'of the Mongols', the same -un as on Qaraγul-un in the first unit. ažuγui is the past 'were'. The opening quotation mark in the English is mine, placed by the reading I explained above.

sentences.t: Hodun-(n)ača olon γaltan keġemüi.
sentences.l: Stars-than many fire-having, it-is-said.
sentences.i: They are said to have more fires than there are stars.
sentences.n: Hodun-(n)ača is hodun 'star' with the ablative -(n)ača, 'from' and in comparison 'than'. olon is 'many'. γaltan is γal 'fire' with -tan, 'having' (Ming 火有的每): 'fire-having', the possessive in a plural form, so 'those with many fires'. keġemüi is the present of keġe- 'say', Ming 說有, 'it is said'. This is the report that the Mongols lit five fires for each man at the end of §193.

sentences.t: Monγol olon ažuγ̇ui.
sentences.l: Mongols many were.
sentences.i: The Mongols were many.
sentences.n: Plain: Moṅγol 'Mongol', olon 'many', ažuγui 'were'. The Ming glosses Moṅγol here, as on Moṅγol-un before, as 達達, 'Tartars', the Ming word for the Mongols; the form is printed here without the dotted ṅ.

sentences.t: Edöġe bida qamtudun baraγ̇asu qaγačaqui berke bolqun-u;
sentences.l: Now we joining if-finished, parting hard becoming-?;
sentences.i: Now, if we once join together, will it be hard to part?
sentences.n: A question, marked by the particle -u in bolqun-u (Ming 做的麽, 'will it be?'). qamtudun baraγasu is 'joining, if-finished' (qamtudun is qamtud- 'join together' with the converb -un, the stem of qamtudγasu in the eighth unit): bara- is 'finish, be spent' (Ming 了呵) and -γasu is the conditional; the sense is 'once we are fully joined', and I have not supplied 'with them', which the Ming leaves out. qaγačaqui is 'parting' (Ming 離的), berke 'hard'. The shape of bolqun is not clear to me: -qun is not a form I can place, so I read the ending as participle + question and no more. The sense, that once the two armies engage it is hard to disengage, fits the Ming but is my reading.

morph.gloss: to join together, be joined (from qamtu 'together'; stem inferred) [相合]

sentences.t: qamtudun baraγ̇asu qara nidun-(n)i-jen hirmes ülü kikün
sentences.l: Joining if-finished, black eyes-own turning not we-shall-do.
sentences.i: Once we are joined, we shall not turn our black eyes aside.
sentences.n: 'Black eyes' is nidun with qara; the Ming 黑眼 reads it plainly. nidun-(n)i-jen carries the accusative -(n)i and then the reflexive -jen, 'our own eyes' (Ming 自的行). hirmes is Ming 轉, 'turn'; I do not know the stem and give it as printed. ülü kikün is 'not do': ülü is the usual negative and kikün is Ming 做咱, 'let us do' (ki- 'do' plus -kün, which the glossary reads as a future participle, 'shall do'; the Ming 咱 adds 'we, let us'). 'We shall not turn our eyes aside' is my reading of the idiom: we shall not flinch. Uncertain.

morph.gloss: to join together, be joined (from qamtu 'together'; stem inferred) [相合]
future participle: shall … (the Ming 咱 adds 'we, let us'; uncertain)

sentences.t: tede qačar(i)-jan qadquγdaγ̇asu qara čisun γaruγ̇asu qaltaril ügei qataṅgin Monγol- dur qamtudγ̇asu bolqu-ju.
sentences.l: Those cheeks-own if-stabbed, black blood if-came-out, avoidance without, stubborn Mongol-at, together-if-joined, becoming-fitting-?
sentences.i: If their cheeks are pierced and black blood comes out, they do not shrink away: is it right to be joined with the stubborn Mongols?
sentences.n: Hard, and I have broken the chain at the semicolons only. tede is 'those' (Ming 那的每), qačar(i)-jan 'cheeks-own' (Ming 腮自的行), qadquγdaγasu is qadqu- 'pierce' + -γda- passive + -γasu 'if' (Ming 被刺呵, 'if stabbed'). The reflexive 'own' points back to the Mongols. qara čisun γaruγasu is 'if black blood comes out' (Ming 出呵). qaltaril ügei is 'without avoidance' (Ming 避無), qataṅgin 'stubborn, hard' (Ming 剛硬). Moṅγol- is printed with a hyphen and the next word is a separate dur, which the Ming glosses 時 'when'; I take dur as the dative-locative on Moṅγol, 'to/with the Mongols'. qamtudγ̇asu bolqu-ju is Ming 相合呵中麽有: 'if joined, is it fitting?'. The Ming's 中 may also be 'will it hit?', so the question may be 'will it do?'. Of the whole unit, the picture of a people who do not flinch when pierced is clear; who is joined with whom is less so.

morph.gloss: to go out, come out [出呵]
Mongol (the hyphen carries it over to the next word) [達達]
dative-locative: at, in (the Ming glosses it 'when') [時]
to become, be fitting [中 麽有]

sentences.t: Moṅγol-un aγtas turuγad keġegdemüi.
sentences.l: Mongols' geldings lean are-said.
sentences.i: The Mongols' geldings are said to be lean.
sentences.n: keġegdemüi is keġe- 'say' with the passive -gde- and the present -müi: Ming 被說有, 'it is said'. The same remark as in the two earlier lines on the geldings. The line returns to the lean geldings that open the speech, which is why I take this to be part of the same argument and not a fresh statement.

sentences.t: Bida ulus(i)-jan Altai dabaγ̇ulun seküġülün ködölžü čerig(i)-jen žibšiġerčü an-i üdüžü jabužu
sentences.l: We, people-own Altai causing-to-cross, causing-to-withdraw, moving, army-own putting-in-order, them luring, going,
sentences.i: Let us bring our people over the Altai, draw them back, move off, put our army in order, lure them on and go,
sentences.n: A converb chain, the first of three units that break one long chain (no full stop falls until bi, two units on): dabaγulun, seküġülün, ködölžü, žibšiġerčü, üdüžü, jabužu. dabaγulun is daba- 'cross (a pass)' with the causative -γul- and -un (Ming 敎越過, 'cause to cross'); seküġülün (Ming 卷退, 'roll back') is the same causative on a stem I take as sekü- 'draw back'. ulus(i)-jan and čerig(i)-jen are 'our own people' and 'our own army' (the reflexive, Ming 自的行). an-i is 'them' (Ming 他每行): an- is the oblique stem of the pronoun and -i the accusative. The finite verb comes at the end of the speech, asγaja 'let us pour', so the whole chain carries the force 'let us …'; I have put 'let us' at the front of the English. The mountain is the Altai (Ming 山名).

morph.gloss: to draw back, roll back (stem uncertain) [卷退]
to put in order, make ready (stem inferred from the printed žibšiġer-) [整搠着]
them (third-person plural oblique stem, inferred) [他(每)行]

sentences.t: Altai-jin ölkes kürtele noγai kerel kerežü jabužu
sentences.l: Altai's foot until-reaching, dog-like quarrel quarrelling going,
sentences.i: all the way to the foot of the Altai, brawling like dogs as we go.
sentences.n: ölkes is Ming 山下, 'foot of a mountain'; Altai-jin ölkes is 'the Altai's foot' and kürtele '-tele' is 'until reaching'. noγai kerel kerežü is 'dog (-like) quarrelling, quarrelling' (the Ming adds 般, 'like', after 狗): kerel is the noun and kerežü the converb of the same root, 'brawling a brawl'. I read it as a running fight on the march; the Mongol says only 'quarrelling like dogs'. jabužu 'going' repeats from the previous unit.

sentences.t: bidan-u aγtas Tarγud bi.
sentences.l: Our geldings fat are.
sentences.i: Our geldings are fat.
sentences.n: bidan-u is 'our', from bida 'we' in its oblique stem bidan- with the genitive -u. aγtas Tarγud: Ming 騸馬每肥每, 'geldings, fat ones'. Tarγud is tarγu 'fat' (an adjective, the stem inferred from the Ming 肥) with the plural -d. bi 'is'. The contrast with the lean Mongol geldings is the point of the plan.

morph.gloss: fat (adjective; stem inferred from the Ming) [肥每]

sentences.t: Keġeli seküġülün Moṅγol-un aγtas biqardaγ̇ulun niγ̇ur deġere an-u asγaja bida" keġežü iležüġüi.
sentences.l: Belly causing-to-draw-up, Mongols' geldings causing-to-weary, face on their pouring-let-us, we" saying, sent-off.
sentences.i: Let us make the bellies draw in and wear out the Mongols' geldings, and pour down on their faces," he said, and sent it off.
sentences.n: The unit closes the speech and the first message. Keġeli is Ming 肚皮, 'belly'; seküġülün 'causing to draw back' (as before) gives 'make the bellies draw in', and whose bellies I cannot say: I take it to be the Mongol geldings', since ours are fat, but the grammar gives only 'belly'. biqardaγulun is biqarda- 'be weary' + causative + converb (Ming 敎疲乏, 'cause to tire'). niγur deġere an-u asγaja is 'upon their face, let us pour', and asγa- (Ming 注) is 'pour out'. The sense, I think, is that we are to pour ourselves down on them when they are worn out, but the image is the Ming's and I am not sure of it. bida closes the speech and is a loose 'we' after the verb. keġežü iležüġüi is 'saying … went/sent' (ile- as before). The closing quotation mark is Shiratori's, printed after bida.

morph.gloss: to draw back, roll back (stem uncertain) [敎抽起]
their, his (third-person genitive, back-vowel form, set after its noun) [他的]

sentences.t: Tere üge-dür Küčülüg Qān ügülerün:
sentences.l: That word-in, Küčülüg Qān speaking:
sentences.i: At those words Küchülüg Qan said:
sentences.n: Tere üge-dür is 'at that word' (Ming 那言語裏, 'in that speech'), with the dative-locative -dür; it takes up the message sent to him in the earlier units. ügülerün is ügüle- 'say' with the converb -rün (Ming 說), and the colon leads to the speech. Küčülüg is Tayang's son and the glosses do not say so here.

sentences.t: "An-a ein eme Tajaṅ žirüge jadarun ene üges ügüležüġüi.
sentences.l: An-a thus woman Tajaṅ heart failing, these words speaking-has.
sentences.i: "And so the woman Tayang, his heart failing, has spoken these words.
sentences.n: Quotation marks open at An-a in Shiratori. An-a is Ming 又, 'again, moreover', which I cannot place; I have rendered it 'And so', carrying the Ming 又 and the 'thus' of ein together; the force is a guess. ein is 'thus'; eme is 'woman' (Ming 妻, 'wife'), and the insult here is that Tayang is a woman; žirüge jadarun is 'heart failing' (Ming 心不能時: jada- 'be unable', -run 'while'). Tajaṅ stands with eme as an apposition, 'the woman Tayang'. ene üges ügüležüġüi 'these words he has said' (the past -žüġüi) closes the sentence at the full stop.

sentences.t: Moṅγol-un olon qaγ̇āča irežüġüi.
sentences.l: Mongols' many from-where came.
sentences.i: From where have the many Mongols come?
sentences.n: Moṅγol-un olon is 'the Mongols' many', a genitive on 'many' that is natural in Mongol (many of the Mongols). qaγ̇āča is Ming 那裏行, 'to/at that place': I split it as qaγa 'where' + -ača, which is my reading, so I take the sentence as a sneering question. The Ming has no question particle, so it may instead be a statement, 'many Mongols have come from there'. irežüġüi 'came' (Ming 來了有).

sentences.t: Moṅγol-un oluṅkin Žamuqa-luγ̇a ende bidan-dur bi.
sentences.l: Mongols' most with-Jamuqa here at-us are.
sentences.i: Most of the Mongols, with Jamuqa, are here among us.
sentences.n: oluṅkin is Ming 多半, 'the greater part', from olon 'many'. Žamuqa-luγa is Jamuqa with the comitative -luγa, 'with'. bidan-dur is 'among us' (dative-locative on the oblique stem of bida). I read it as Küchülüg's point that the greater part of the Mongols, those who follow Jamuqa, are on the Naiman side, so the enemy is not as numerous as the scouts say.

morph.gloss: the greater part, most (from olon 'many') [多半]
Jamuqa, a man's name [人名 一同]
the pronoun's linking n plus dative-locative -dur: at, among

sentences.t: Kündü eme-jin čiġeküi γažar-a ese γaruγsan
sentences.l: Heavy woman's urinating place-to not gone-out,
sentences.i: One who has never gone out as far as the place where a heavy woman makes water,
sentences.n: Kündü is Ming 重, 'heavy', and I take it of a pregnant woman. čiġeküi (Ming 尿處) is 'passing water' with a participle; the stem čiġe- is inferred from the Ming. The phrase is a jibe: a man who has not been farther than where a pregnant woman goes to relieve herself, that is, he has never left camp. γaruγsan is a past participle and qualifies eme, the last word of the next unit: 'the woman who has not gone out …'. The English keeps the Mongol order and supplies no subject. Colourful and uncertain.

morph.gloss: heavy, weighty (here of a pregnant woman) [重]
to pass water (stem inferred from the Ming 尿處) [尿處]
to go out, come out [出的]
past participle: the one who has … (u a linking vowel)

sentences.t: kürdün-ü tuγul-un belžiġel-dür ese kürügsen eme
sentences.l: Cart-wheel's calf's grazing-at not reached woman,
sentences.i: who has never come to where the cart-wheel's calf grazes, a woman —
sentences.n: kürdün is Ming 車腳, 'cart foot', and I take it as the wheel; kürdün-ü tuγul-un is 'the cart-wheel's calf's', two genitives in a row, and belžiġel-dür is 'at the grazing' (Ming 喫草行). The picture, as I read it, is of calves tethered by the cart near the tent, as if he had never gone farther than that. kürügsen is the past participle of kür- 'reach', with ese 'not'. eme 'woman' ends the unit and is the noun that kürügsen and the earlier γaruγsan qualify; Ming 婦人.

morph.gloss: cart-wheel (the Ming has 車腳, 'cart foot') [車腳的]
past participle: the one who has …

sentences.t: Tajaṅ žirüge jadarun ese-ü"
sentences.l: Tajaṅ heart failing not?"
sentences.i: Tayang, his heart failing: is it not so?"
sentences.n: The same žirüge jadarun 'heart failing' as in Küchülüg's taunt earlier in this section. ese-ü is Ming 不曾, 'not', with a final -ü that I take as a question; so 'is it not so?' The closing quotation mark is Shiratori's. The three units from 'Kündü eme-jin' on form one sentence, which I have split into three readable units.

sentences.t: ede üges ügüležü irežüġüi keġen
sentences.l: These words speaking, came, saying,
sentences.i: These words, once spoken, came; so saying,
sentences.n: ede üges ügüležü is 'these words, speaking' (Ming 這言語每說着), irežüġüi 'came' (Ming 來了有) and keġen the converb 'saying' (Ming 麽道). This is the hardest joint in the part. The subject of 'came' is not stated, and the Ming gives no help: it may be Küchülüg's reported speech that comes (he has said these words), or the envoys who come back. The English follows the first, but it is a guess.

sentences.t: elčin-eče ečige-jüġen eberetele bertetele ügüležü iležüküi.
sentences.l: From-envoys father-own pain-until wound-until speaking, sent.
sentences.i: he sent word through the envoys to his own father, speaking until it pained and wounded.
sentences.n: elčin-eče is 'envoy' (Ming 使臣行) with the ablative -eče, 'from' and here 'by'. ečige-jüġen is 'to his own father' (reflexive -jüġen, Ming 父自的行). eberetele and bertetele are two -tele forms, 'until it aches' and 'until it wounds' (Ming 痛 and 傷); the stems ebere- and berte- are as the Ming reads them. The two final verbs are 'speaking, went/sent' (ile- again; -žüküi). This is Küchülüg's message to Tayang, as its effect in the next unit shows.

morph.gloss: to be in pain, ache (Ming 痛) [痛]
to be hurt, wounded (Ming 傷) [傷]

sentences.t: Ene üge-dür Tajaṅ Qān öġer(i)-jen emečilegden ügülegdežü Tajaṅ Qān ügülerün:
sentences.l: This word-in, Tajaṅ Qān himself-own woman-treated-being-said, Tajaṅ Qān speaking:
sentences.i: At these words Tayang Qan, himself treated as a woman and spoken of so, said:
sentences.n: emečilegden is eme 'woman' + -či- + -le- ('treat as') + the passive -gde- + the converb -n: 'being made a woman of' (Ming 被做婦人); the stem is as the Ming reads it. ügülegdežü is 'being spoken of' (Ming 被說着). öġer(i)-jen is Ming (自己)自的行, 'his own self': the (i) is Shiratori's, and I take it as the patient of the two passives, 'himself'. The Mongol names no one who does the calling, so neither does the English. The colon leads into Tayang's speech, whose opening mark comes at the next word.

morph.gloss: to treat as a woman, make a woman of (from eme) [被做婦人]

sentences.t: "Küčütü omoγtu Küčülüg kürülčeküi alalduqui üdür maqa ene omog(i)-jan bu talbituγai.
sentences.l: Strength-having, bravery-having Küčülüg, meeting killing-each-other day, perhaps this bravery-own not let-go!
sentences.i: "Küchülüg is strong and brave: on the day of meeting and killing one another, may he not let go of this bravery of his!
sentences.n: Küčütü and omoγtu are küčü 'strength' and omoγ 'bravery' with the possessive -tü/-tu, 'strength-having', 'bravery-having' (Ming 氣力有的, 勇有的); the pattern is the possessive of the previous parts. kürülčeküi alalduqui üdür is 'the day of meeting, of killing one another' (Ming 到的, 相殺的): kür- 'reach', -ülče- the reciprocal, ala- 'kill' with -ldu- 'each other'. maqa is Ming 莫不 'perhaps (not)', which in this mood I render 'may he not'. omog(i)-jan is 'his own bravery' (reflexive). bu talbituγai is 'let him not put down', the prohibitive bu with the optative -tuγai (Ming 休放了者). The sense, as I read it, is that Tayang answers the insult by praising his son's courage and hoping he will not lose it on the day.

morph.gloss: to meet, come together (from kür- 'reach') [到的]
to let go, leave, put down [放了者︀]

sentences.t: Kürülčen qamtudun baraγ̇asu qaγačaqui maqa berke bi-že" keġebe.
sentences.l: Meeting, joining if-finished, parting perhaps hard is," he-said.
sentences.i: If we meet and are once joined, perhaps it will be hard to part," he said.
sentences.n: Kürülčen is the converb 'meeting' (Ming 相到); qamtudun baraγasu 'once joined' and qaγačaqui 'parting' repeat from the question earlier, now with maqa 'perhaps' (Ming 莫不) and berke 'hard'. bi-že is 'is' with an assertive particle (Ming 有也者), and keġebe 'said' (Ming 說了). The words echo what Tayang said to Küchülüg in the first message. The English adds nothing to 'meeting' and 'joined', as in the earlier question.

morph.gloss: to join together, be joined (from qamtu 'together'; stem inferred) [相合]
to be, there is (stem bi- before -že) [有也者︀]

sentences.t: Tere üge-dür Tajaṅ Qān-(n)u doro medekü jeke nojan Qori-Sübeči ügülerün:
sentences.l: That word-in, Tajaṅ Qān's below managing great lord Qori-Sübeči speaking:
sentences.i: At those words Qori-Sübechi, Tayang Qan's great lord, who had charge of those below, said:
sentences.n: doro medekü jeke nojan is Ming 下管的大官人, 'the great lord who manages below'. doro is 'below, lower'; medekü is the participle of mede- 'know', glossed 管 'manage'. I have rendered it 'who had charge of those below', which is my reading and nothing more: doro may as well name his rank as the people under him, and medekü is a participle, not a past 'held'. Tajaṅ Qān-(n)u is one printed word, the genitive -(n)u on a title after a name. ügülerün: the colon leads into Qori-Sübechi's speech, which Shiratori opens at the next word.

morph.gloss: Tayang, a man's name [人名 皇帝的]
to know, manage, have charge of [管的]

sentences.t: "Inanča-Bilge Qān ečige čin-u sača nökör-e ere-jin aru aγta-jin qarγam ese üžeġülüleġe.
sentences.l: Inanča-Bilge Qān father your alike companions-to, men's back, geldings' hindquarters not caused-to-see.
sentences.i: "Inancha-Bilge Qan, your father, never let his companions see the backs of his men or the rumps of his geldings.
sentences.n: Spoken to Tayang; the 'your father' is Inancha-Bilge Qan, the previous ruler of the Naiman. Inanča-Bilge Qān ečige čin-u is 'Inancha-Bilge Qan, your father' (čin-u is the genitive of či 'you'). nökör-e is 'to companions' (Ming 伴當行) and sača is Ming 一般, 'alike, equally', which I cannot place, and have left it out of the English. ere-jin aru and aγta-jin qarγam are 'the man's back' and 'the gelding's hindquarters' (Ming 脊背, 後胯), the genitive -jin after a vowel. Ese üžeġülüleġe is 'did not make see': üže- 'see', causative -ġül-, past -leġe. The sense, I take it, is that the old khan never turned his back in retreat before his men and so never showed the rumps of retreating horses. The Ming says nothing of retreat; it is my reading.

morph.gloss: hindquarters, rump (Ming 後胯, 'hind hip') [後胯]

sentences.t: Edöġe či manaγar erte böġed jakin žirüge jadamu či.
sentences.l: Now you dawn early already how heart failing-do you.
sentences.i: Now, how is it that you lose heart so early, at the very dawn?
sentences.n: Edöġe is 'now'; či 'you'. manaγar erte böġed is a run of time words: manaγar 'dawn, early morning' (Ming 淸), erte 'early' (Ming 早), böġed (Ming 便, 'already, then'). I read it as 'as early as dawn', that is, at the very start. jakin is 'how, why' (Ming 如何). žirüge jadamu 'heart fails' (Ming 不能有), present tense. The final či repeats 'you' at the end of the sentence, which is printed with a full stop. The English 'at the very dawn' leans on the Ming 淸早, 'clear, early morning'; it is my gloss.

morph.gloss: ending of uncertain force: a particle of sequence, 'then, already' (meaning inferred from the Ming 便)

sentences.t: čima-ji ein žirüge jadaqui-ji medegsen böġesü
sentences.l: You-ACC thus heart failing-one-ACC known having if,
sentences.i: If I had known you to be one of such failing heart,
sentences.n: čima-ji and jadaqui-ji both carry the accusative -ji (Ming 行): 'you' and 'the one who fails', the object of medegsen 'having known' (Ming 知道了). böġesü is the conditional of bü- 'be' (Ming 有呵), 'if it be'. So 'if I had known you, the one who thus fails in heart'. The unit is a clause that waits for its main verb in the next.

morph.gloss: to be unable, fail [不能的行]

sentences.t: qatun ber küġün böġesü eke-ji čin-u Kürbesü-ji abčiražü čerig ülü-ü žasaγ̇ulqu büleġe.
sentences.l: Lady also person if-be, mother your Kürbesü bringing-along, army not-?? cause-to-order was.
sentences.i: if the lady too is a person, would one not, bringing your mother Kürbesü along, have had the army put in order?
sentences.n: Hard. qatun ber küġün böġesü is 'if the lady too is a person' (Ming 娘子也人有呵); qatun is 'lady' and may be Kürbesü herself (§§189–190 call her 'our Lady'), but Kürbesü-ji is the object of abčiražü and the bringing-along has no stated subject; I read the line as 'even a lady who is a person would have had the army put in order'. eke-ji čin-u Kürbesü-ji is 'mother-ACC your Kürbesü-ACC' (Ming 母行, 母名行), two accusatives in apposition. abčiražü is 'bringing along' (Ming 將來着). ülü-ü žasaγulqu büleġe is 'not-? to-cause-to-order was' (Ming 不敎整治有來): the final -ü is the question, so 'would she not have had it ordered?'. The use of the question is my reading; the Ming 不 is the plain negative. Kürbesü is the name used in §§189–190. The sentence does not close with a full stop in the print, so its grammar remains open to a different reading.

morph.gloss: lady, queen, wife of a ruler [娘子]
Kürbesü, a woman's name [母名 行]
to take along, bring (Ming 將來) [將來着]
to order, put in order [敎整治]

sentences.t: Čima qailan Kögseġü-Sabraγ ötöldeküi.
sentences.l: Čima! pity Kögseġü-Sabraγ grown-old.
sentences.i: Alas, what a pity! Kökse'ü-Sabraq has grown old.
sentences.n: Čima is Ming 嘆聲, 'exclamation', although čima is elsewhere the oblique stem of 'you' (čima-ji, čima-dur); the Ming here takes it as a sigh, and I follow it. qailan is Ming 可惜, 'pity'. Kögseġü-Sabraγ is the name that appears as Kökse'ü-Sabraq in §§189–190. ötöldeküi is Ming 被老了, 'has grown old', from ötöl- 'grow old' with an ending -de- that I cannot place. Who is lamenting, and why the age matters, the grammar does not say.

morph.gloss: you (oblique stem čima-; the Ming takes it here as an exclamation) [嘆聲]
to cry out (here the exclamation 'alas, what a pity'; uncertain) [可惜]
participle (here 'has …', after the Ming 被老了)

sentences.t: Jaγ̇un čerig-ün bidan-u žasal sülberküi bolbi.
sentences.l: What army's our rule slack has-become.
sentences.i: Why has the discipline of our army grown slack?
sentences.n: Jaγun is Ming 甚麽, 'what, why'; čerig-ün bidan-u žasal is 'army's our rule' (the genitives in a row, Ming 軍的咱的法度); sülberküi is Ming 怠慢, 'slack, remiss'; bolbi is the past 'has become'. The Ming has no question particle, so 'why' is my choice; 'what! our army's rule has become slack' is the other reading.

sentences.t: Moṅγol-un čaγ žajaγ̇an bi-že;
sentences.l: Mongols' time fortune is;
sentences.i: The Mongols have their hour and their fortune;
sentences.n: čaγ is 'time' (Ming 時) and žajaγan 'fate, fortune' (Ming 氣運). bi-že is 'is' with the assertive particle (Ming 有也者). The semicolon sets the clause off from the one that follows. I read the line as the speaker saying that the Mongols' time has come (or that they have luck), but the Mongol states only that they have a time and a fortune.

morph.gloss: to be, there is (stem bi- before -že) [有也者︀]

sentences.t: ese bolbi.
sentences.l: not become.
sentences.i: and it has not yet come right.
sentences.n: ese bolbi is Ming 不曾中了, 'not (past) hit/right': ese 'not' and bolbi 'has become'. I read 'has not come right', that is, the Mongols' fortune has not yet come off; or perhaps our fortune has not. The Ming 中 (to hit) can also mean 'it did not hit the mark'. Uncertain, and I have left the subject out of the English as the Mongol does.

sentences.t: Ai! Turluγ Tajaṅ jadaqu metü ele bijü či" kēġed
sentences.l: Ai! Turluγ Tajaṅ failing-one like only are you," saying,
sentences.i: Ah! Turluγ Tayang, you are only the sort that fails," he said,
sentences.n: Ai is a sigh (Ming 唉). Turluγ has no Ming gloss, as in §§189–190, where it stands beside Tayang as an epithet; I leave it in the English. jadaqu metü ele bijü či is 'failing-one like only is you' (Ming 不能的般但有你): jadaqu is the participle 'the one who fails', metü 'like' (Ming 般), ele 'only' (Ming 但), bijü 'is'. The closing quotation mark is Shiratori's. It ends Qori-Sübechi's speech, which began with Inancha-Bilge's name. kēġed is keġe- 'say' with -ġed, 'having said'.

morph.gloss: (sense unknown: the Ming gives no gloss, it stands beside Tayang as an epithet)

sentences.t: qor(i)-jan deledüġed buruγ̇u qataraba.
sentences.l: Quiver-own striking, buruγu, spurred-off.
sentences.i: and striking his quiver he rode off.
sentences.n: qor(i)-jan is 'his own quiver' (Ming 箭筒自的行). deledüġed is Ming 打着, 'striking', from a stem I take as deledü-. buruγu is a word the Ming glosses with a single rare character, 𠮠, which I cannot read (it is one of the characters outside the ordinary range, as in §§1–6), so I leave it out of the English. qataraba is Ming 點着去了, 'went off at a dig': qatara- 'spur, gallop' plus the past -ba. The part ends with Qori-Sübechi leaving the council.

morph.gloss: quiver (the (i) is Shiratori's linking vowel) [箭筒自的行]
to strike (stem as printed, Ming 打) [打着]
(sense uncertain: the Ming gives a single character, 𠮠, which I cannot read) [𠮠]
to spur, gallop (Ming 點着去, 'went off at a dig') [點着去了]
